The Kingdom of Dahomey was a powerful West African state that existed from the early 1600s until French colonization in 1894, located in what is now southern Benin. Starting as a smaller inland kingdom, it expanded to control important coastal trading centers like Ouidah and became one of the most centralized states in pre-colonial Africa, with kings exercising direct authority over trade, taxation, and military affairs through a sophisticated bureaucracy. The kingdom gained prominence for its professional army, including the famous female warrior units known to Europeans as the Dahomey Amazons, and its active participation in the Atlantic slave trade, which fueled much of its economic prosperity. Throughout the 18th and 19th centuries, Dahomey frequently waged wars against neighboring states such as the Oyo Empire and the Kingdom of Savè, both to capture slaves for export and to expand territorial control. The kingdom reached its peak under rulers like Ghezo and Glélé in the mid-1800s, but increasing European interference weakened its position, and after two wars with France in the 1890s, the last king Béhanzin was defeated and exiled in 1894, bringing an end to Dahomey's independence and leading to its incorporation into French West Africa.
Kingdom of save
The Kingdom of Savè (or Sabé in Yoruba) was a Yoruba kingdom that sat right on the border between what's now Benin and Nigeria. It came together in the mid-1700s when a leader named Yai managed to unite a bunch of different city-states that had been there for centuries—some founded by earlier Yoruba migrants, others by groups fleeing the collapse of the Songhai Empire. The kingdom had its moments of stability, especially under King Akinkanju who set up a council system and got involved in the slave trade through Porto Novo, but it was always kind of vulnerable because of its location.
Conquest
When Akinkanju became the fifth king, things actually settled down for a while. He set up a council made up of different lineage leaders and grew the kingdom's wealth by getting involved in the slave trade with Porto Novo. But the problem was that Savè was kind of exposed geographically, so it kept facing threats from outside no matter what. Things took a bad turn in 1828 when Dahomey's King Ghézo executed around thirty prisoners from Savè after a raid, which obviously destroyed any goodwill between the two kingdoms. Then starting in the mid-1800s, Fulani jihadists kept attacking and weakening Savè even more. The late 1800s were worse. Dahomey increased its attacks. The capital got completely wiped out in 1848, then they rebuilt it, and it got destroyed again in 1855. They kept trying to rebuild, but the raids just wouldn't stop. Finally in 1885, Dahomey launched one last massive attack that leveled the capital for good, and that was basically the end of Savè as an independent kingdom. Dahomey's King Glélé put someone loyal to him on the throne, and by 1894, it was under French protectorate, as Dahomey was conquered by the French.
